name: Read-Write Lock
intent: Let many threads read shared data at the same time, but give a writer exclusive access.
scenario: A configuration cache is read thousands of times a second by many threads and changed only once in a while.
problem: One plain lock guards the cache, so readers take turns even though reading does not change anything. Most of the threads spend their time waiting for each other, and the cache becomes the slowest part of the program.
solution: A ReadWriteLock has two modes. Any number of readers can hold it together, as long as nobody is writing. A writer needs the lock to itself: it waits until the readers have left, and while it holds the lock new readers wait. Readers do not block one another, so read-heavy code scales with the number of threads, and writes stay safe. The policy for who goes next decides whether writers can starve.
pain: Readers wait for each other, though reading changes nothing
Throughput stays flat as threads are added
The lock is held by readers for nearly all of the time
A simple mutex cannot tell a reader from a writer
benefits: Readers run in parallel, so read-heavy workloads scale with threads
Writers still get exclusive, safe access
Readers always see a consistent value, never a half-written one
The code states its intent: this part only reads, this part changes
whenToUse: Shared data is read much more often than it is written
Reads take long enough that running them together matters
Readers must see consistent data and writers must not be interleaved
whenNotToUse: Writes are common: the extra bookkeeping makes it slower than a plain mutex
Critical sections are very short: lock overhead costs more than waiting
Data that can be replaced as an immutable snapshot: swap the reference instead of locking
pitfalls: Writer starvation: if readers keep arriving, a writer that waits for zero readers may never get in
A read that also changes something, such as a hit counter, is a write and races with other readers
Upgrading from a read lock to a write lock while holding it can deadlock
In single-threaded runtimes such as plain JavaScript there is no parallel access to guard

roles.label: Read-write lock
roles.description: Tracks how many readers hold it and whether a writer does, and decides who may enter.

roles.label: Reader
roles.description: Takes the lock in shared mode to look at the data. Many readers may be inside at once.

roles.label: Writer
roles.description: Takes the lock in exclusive mode to change the data. Nobody else is inside while it holds it.

roles.label: Shared data
roles.description: The configuration or cache that the lock protects.

quiz.question: A configuration cache is read about 5,000 times a second by 16 threads and updated once a minute. A mutex guards it, and the threads spend most of their time waiting. What is the best change?
options: Add more threads, so that more of them are ready when the mutex is released
Keep the mutex, but make the cache a global variable so that access is quicker
Use a read-write lock, so that the readers can hold it together and only writes are exclusive
Remove the lock, since the update happens so rarely that two threads will not meet
quiz.explanation: Reading does not change the data, so readers need not exclude each other. A read-write lock lets all 16 read together and keeps writes safe. More threads wait more, a global does not change the locking, and removing the lock allows a read to see a half-written update.

quiz.question: During a busy hour a configuration update waits for minutes, because new readers keep arriving before the old ones leave. What is the best fix?
options: Use a fair or writer-preferring policy, so that new readers wait once a writer is queued
Add a sleep before every read, so that there are short gaps between the readers
Let the writer change the data without the lock when it has waited longer than a minute
Make the readers hold the lock for longer, so that the writer is easier to notice
quiz.explanation: With a readers-first policy a writer can starve. A fair policy lets the current readers finish and then admits the writer before newer readers. Sleeps only slow the readers, writing without the lock corrupts data, and longer holds make the wait worse.

quiz.question: A developer adds a hit counter inside the read-locked section of a cache, 'because it is only a read'. Under load the counts are wrong. What is the explanation?
options: The read lock is too slow, so some of the counts are dropped on the way
The counter is stored in a different place from the data and so is not protected at all
The counter should be larger, since a small number type loses counts under heavy load
Many readers run together, so updating a shared counter inside the read lock is an unprotected race
quiz.explanation: The read lock lets many threads in at once, so two of them can update the counter at the same time and lose an increment. Changing shared state is a write. Use an atomic counter, or keep the counter outside the data's lock.
